lesson.menu_title: Drawing the Org Chart Out Loud
lesson.menu_desc: Describing a group, a reporting line and a decision in one sentence, without losing the listener -- 38 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 6 -- Drawing the Org Chart Out Loud
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Fernando Meneghelli Bottura | Lesson 6 -- Drawing the Org Chart Out Loud

listenings.text: People assume that when a panel asks about your reporting line they are checking a fact. They are not. The fact is on your CV. What they are testing is whether you understand where power actually sat, and whether you can say it out loud without complaining about it. In a matrix everybody has two bosses and the interesting question is never who signs your objectives. It is who you go to when the two of them disagree. Candidates who describe the chart and stop there sound junior, because a chart is public information. Candidates who describe the chart and then tell you which line was the real one, and how they knew, sound like people who have run something. And by the way, the tone matters more than the content here. The moment a description of a structure turns into a complaint about a structure, we stop hearing an executive and start hearing somebody who did not fit.

What I walked into was a holding company with four subsidiaries, two of which had been acquired eighteen months earlier and had never really been integrated. My formal reporting line was to the group chief executive, who was based in London, and I had a dotted line to the group finance director, who was the person who actually decided things. That distinction cost me about six months to work out. The business units each had their own controller, which sounded sensible on paper and meant in practice that nobody owned a consolidated number. The shared service centre we eventually built was not my idea, and I will say that clearly because people always assume it was. It came from one of the controllers, whose team was doing the same reconciliation four times a month for four different entities.

extra_audio.text: Claire describes the client group as a holding company with three subsidiaries. Claire explains that the reporting line runs to Brussels and there is a dotted line to the chief executive. Fernando asks which of the two lines actually decides. Claire says that is the right question and gives him the answer. Fernando describes the structure he inherited in his own group in one sentence.

reading.rtitle: What an org chart question is really asking
paras: Every senior interview contains a question about structure. Who did you report to, how many people reported to you, how were the entities organized. Candidates treat it as a factual question and answer it factually, and that is the first mistake, because the facts are already on the CV that got them into the room.

The question is about navigation. A chart describes where authority is supposed to sit. Anyone who has run a finance function inside a group knows that where it actually sits is a different map, learned slowly and never written down. A candidate who can describe both maps, calmly, has demonstrated something no reference check can confirm.

There is a trap in the second map, and it is tone. The distance between explaining a structure and complaining about a structure is one adjective wide. The panel is listening for it, because a CFO who describes a matrix as unworkable is telling them how they will describe theirs in two years.

The strongest version is short and specific. Name the formal line. Name the informal one. Say how you worked out which was which, and give one example of a decision that went the way it did because of it. Four sentences, no adjectives, and the panel has learned more about you than from the whole of the rest of the interview.

gist.prompt: What is the main point of this text?
choices: Panels ask about structure to verify the facts on the candidate's CV.
The question tests whether you can describe where power really sat, without complaining about it.
Matrix structures are unworkable and candidates should say so honestly.

items: The facts about a reporting line are usually already known to the panel.
The text says they are on the CV that got the candidate into the room.
A chart shows where authority actually sits.
It shows where authority is SUPPOSED to sit. The real map is learned slowly and never written down.
The difference between explaining and complaining is described as very small.
One adjective wide, according to the text.
Calling a matrix unworkable makes a candidate sound experienced.
It tells the panel how the candidate will describe THEIR structure in two years.
The strongest answer includes one decision that went a particular way because of the informal line.
Formal line, informal line, how you worked it out, and one example.
